title: Differentiation rules and the chain rule
terms: sum rule; constant multiple rule; product rule; quotient rule; chain rule; composite derivative.

What is the derivative at x = 0 of F (x) = e log(2 + cos x)?
(A) 0 (B) 1/3 (C) log 2 (D) log 3 (E) 1 + log 3

solution.text:
′ sin x sin x
The product rule gives F = e cos x log(2 + cos x) − e sin x/(2 + cos x). At zero the
second term vanishes and the first is log 3.

question.text:
A differentiable f : R → R satisfies f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) for all real x, y, with f (0) = 1 and
′
f (0) = 3. Which identity follows?
′ ′
(A) f (x) = 3 (B) f (x) = 3f(x)
′ 3 ′
(C) f (x) = f (x) (D) f (x) = 3xf (x)
′
(E) f (x) = f (x)/3

solution.text:
′
Fix x and differentiate the identity with respect to y at y = 0. The left derivative is f (x),
′
while the right derivative is f(x)f (0) = 3f (x). The parameter held fixed contributes no
derivative factor.

question.text:
Let u(x) = |x| and v(x) = x|x|. Which statement about the product u(x)v(x) at zero is correct?
(A) It is not differentiable because u is not.
(B) It is differentiable with derivative 1.
(C) It is differentiable with derivative 0, even though the product rule cannot be invoked using
′
u (0).
(D) It is discontinuous.
(E) Its derivative has unequal one-sided limits at zero.

solution.text:
3
The product simplifies exactly to x , so its derivative at zero is 0. The usual product rule is
′
sufficient when both factors are differentiable, but u (0) does not exist here. Algebra or the
definition must establish the derivative instead.
